What they did: dataset-example maximization, judged by eye. For a unit they take x' = argmax over x in I of <φ(x), e_i>, where I is a held-out set and e_i is the natural basis vector of hidden unit i. For a random direction they take x' = argmax over x in I of <φ(x), v>, for "any random direction v ∈ R^n". The paper does not say how v is drawn: no distribution, no normalization, no orthogonalization. The captions say "random basis", but the text only ever speaks of single random directions. φ(x) is defined as "activation values of some layer". The Introduction says the claim concerns "the units of the last feature layer", but the paper never names the layer for either network, and never says whether φ is taken before or after the ReLU.

Models and data:
(1) MNIST. Section 3 says "a convolutional neural network trained on MNIST", with the MNIST test set as I. This conflicts with Section 2, which lists only fully connected (FC) and autoencoder (AE) networks for MNIST, and with Section 4.2, which says "For MNIST, we do not have results for convolutional models yet".
(2) AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al.) on ImageNet, with the ImageNet validation set as I.

Evidence: four figures only.
- Fig. 1 (MNIST, 4 units) and Fig. 2 (MNIST, 4 random directions): each row holds 10 digits.
- Fig. 3 (AlexNet, 4 units) and Fig. 4 (AlexNet, 4 random directions): each row holds 5 whole validation images.
- Each row carries a hand-written label, e.g. "Unit sensitive to white flowers.", "Direction sensitive to white dogs.".

What is missing: no number of units or directions examined, no rater protocol, no blinding, no held-out or predictive test, no quantitative score of any kind. The conclusion rests on the authors' visual judgment that "the resulting images share many high-level similarities". The source archive holds 8 unit rows and 8 random-direction rows for ImageNet, of which 4 of each are printed: units 2, 6, 7, 8 and directions 1, 3, 4, 6. The paper does not say how those were chosen. The rest of the paper (Sections 4 to 4.3) covers adversarial examples and Lipschitz bounds, and has nothing further on units versus directions.
numbers: Units vs random directions: the paper reports zero quantitative measurements. There is no score, rate, count of units or directions examined, or significance test. The only quantity in the claim is 'for many x′'.
MNIST (Figs. 1-2): 4 unit rows and 4 random-direction rows are shown. Each row has 10 digits (source images are 300x28 px).
AlexNet/ImageNet (Figs. 3-4): 4 unit rows and 4 random-direction rows are shown. Each row has 5 validation images (source images are 1150x224 px, five 224-px tiles).

The TeX source holds 8 ImageNet unit rows (natural_imagenet_1..8) and 8 random-direction rows (random_imagenet_1..8). The printed figures use units 2, 6, 7, 8 and directions 1, 3, 4, 6. The paper does not state how they were selected.

My own pixel comparison of the figure tiles (this is not stated in the paper): the top-1 and top-2 images of Unit 3(a) 'white flowers' are pixel-identical to the top-1 and top-2 images of random Direction 4(a) 'white, spread flowers'. The same two images also appear at positions 5 and 2 of random Direction 4(c) 'spread shapes'. So 2 of the 4 printed random directions share 2 of their 5 shown images with one printed unit. Separately, the unprinted unit row natural_imagenet_3 shares its position-2 image with Unit 3(d) (natural_imagenet_8).
Held-out sets used as I: the MNIST test set and the ImageNet validation set.
Networks in Section 2: FC and AE on MNIST, AlexNet on ImageNet, and QuocNet (~1 billion parameters, ~10M YouTube images). QuocNet is not used in Section 3.
Paper versions: v1 21 Dec 2013, v2 3 Jan 2014, v3 13 Feb 2014, v4 19 Feb 2014. 10 pages, no appendix.

Numbers elsewhere in the paper concern adversarial examples, not units, and are listed only for completeness. AlexNet average distortion is 0.006508 over 64 examples (Fig. 5). Tables 1-4 give MNIST distortions of 0.058-0.14 and cross-model errors. Table 5 gives AlexNet layer Lipschitz upper bounds from 2.75 to 11.

read:szegedy2013.bearing:
Overall: the paper supports our finding but contributes no measurement of its own. It is the original, qualitative statement of the same claim. Our blind audit is a quantitative replication of that claim, on a different network and with stricter tests.

1. Where it agrees: pre-ReLU, both layers. The paper's headline is that there is "no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units", and that "the natural basis is not better than a random basis". Our numbers match this: 40 units vs 40 random unit-norm pre-ReLU directions score alike on 'one job' at mixed5b (0.57 vs 0.68) and mixed4c (0.79 vs 0.74). Their evidence is 4+4 rows on MNIST and 4+4 rows on AlexNet, judged by the authors' own eyes with no numbers. Ours is n=40+40 per layer, rated blind, and adds a held-out predictive test. So we supply the measurement the paper lacks; the paper does not independently confirm our numbers. Its claim covers "high level"/"last feature layer" units. mixed5b, the last Inception block of InceptionV1, falls in that scope; mixed4c, a middle layer, goes beyond it.

2. Where the paper cannot reach: post-ReLU. The paper defines φ(x) only as "activation values of some layer". It never says which layer, or whether φ is taken before or after the ReLU, and never says how v is drawn. If AlexNet's φ was post-ReLU, which is plausible but unstated, then our post-ReLU result partly disagrees with the strong 'no distinction' claim: random post-ReLU directions score lower on the held-out description test. Even so, our post-ReLU directions do not score lower on the 'one job' rating. That rating is roughly the only kind of judgment the paper made. The paper's eyeball method had no held-out test and so could not have seen this difference. It neither contradicts nor supports our post-ReLU result. The paper never uses the term 'privileged basis'. Its nearest notion is "distinguished basis", which it rejects for the last feature layer. It gives no mechanism, such as the ReLU, by which units could become privileged.

3. The confound our overlap check addresses. The paper's own printed figures show the problem. In my pixel comparison of the figure tiles (not stated in the paper), random Direction 4(a) shares its top-2 images with Unit 3(a), and random Direction 4(c) contains the same two images. The authors' commented-out draft text predicted this: high-norm outlier images are extreme under many random projections, "where the same sample appears on different random directions". So the paper's demonstration cannot rule out that its random directions inherit their apparent meaning from a few dominant units or high-norm images. Our median top-16 overlap of 2 of 16 with any single unit is exactly the check the paper never ran, and it rules out the 'a unit in disguise' reading for our directions. It does not test the other half of the confound, high-norm images shared across random directions. A useful follow-up would be to measure overlap among our 40 random directions, and between each direction and the top images ranked by ||φ(x)||.

4. Differences in setup that limit direct comparison:
- Network: AlexNet, plus an MNIST net whose description is inconsistent in the paper, vs our InceptionV1 (inception5h).
- Images: whole validation images, 5 per row (10 for MNIST), vs our 28 dataset-example crops.
- Who judges: the authors, unblinded, vs blind Haiku raters plus a judge.
- Rows shown: 4 of 8 available rows per basis, selection unexplained, vs our 40 per arm.

The 'rotation' language comes only from the Mikolov word-vector analogy in the Introduction. The paper itself tests no rotated orthonormal basis, only individual random directions.
read:szegedy2013.caveats:
1. The paper gives only a qualitative visual demonstration. Every 'number' about units vs directions is a count of figure rows or images, not a measurement.
2. The MNIST network is described inconsistently. Section 3 says "convolutional neural network trained on MNIST"; Section 2 lists only FC and AE networks for MNIST; Section 4.2 says there are no convolutional MNIST results yet.
3. The layer, the pre- vs post-nonlinearity choice, and the distribution of v (Gaussian? unit-norm? orthogonalized?) are all unspecified.
4. The duplicate-image finding comes from my own pixel comparison of the figure PNGs in the arXiv source (identical after resizing to 64x64, mean absolute difference 0.0). The paper does not state it.
5. The heavy-tail and outlier quotes, and "laying on a rim of the manifold", are from text commented out in the TeX source. They are not in any published version.
6. I fetched the paper with curl rather than WebFetch. The content is the arXiv v4 PDF and the official e-print source.
7. Later work that disputes this claim using feature visualization rather than dataset examples (e.g. Olah et al. 2017) was not read here. Nothing about it is asserted from this paper.

read:bau2017.method:
**Scoring units (Sec. 2.2).** Each convolutional unit k is treated as a binary segmenter and checked against every concept in Broden. Broden merges ADE, OpenSurfaces, Pascal-Context, Pascal-Part, DTD and generated color labels, with pixel-level masks except for scenes and textures. Fig. 3 counts 1197 segmentation tasks.
- Activations are collected over all of Broden.
- A per-unit threshold T_k is set at the top 0.005 quantile over all spatial locations.
- Activation maps are bilinearly upsampled to mask resolution and thresholded to M_k(x).
- IoU_{k,c} = sum|M_k ∩ L_c| / sum|M_k ∪ L_c| over the whole dataset.
- A unit counts as a detector if IoU > 0.04, and it takes its top-ranked label.
- Layer interpretability is the "number of unique detectors": the count of distinct concepts that some unit matches. It is not the fraction of interpretable units.

**Rotation experiment (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 4).**
- Model and layer: one model and one layer, the 256 conv5 units of AlexNet trained from scratch on Places205.
- Rotation: one random orthogonal Q drawn uniformly (Haar) from SO(256), by Gram-Schmidt / QR of a Gaussian 256x256 matrix with a positive-diagonal R, following Diaconis. Each rotated "unit" is a row of Q, so it is a uniformly random unit-norm direction, and the 256 directions are mutually orthogonal.
- Scoring: Qf(x) gets the same dissection and the unique detectors are counted.
- Partial rotations: Q^alpha for alpha in {0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1}, a minimal geodesic from I to Q computed by Schur decomposition.
- Discriminative power: argued to be unchanged because g'(r) = g(Q^T r).

**What the paper does not state.**
- Whether f(x) = "AlexNet conv5" is taken before or after the ReLU.
- How many rotation draws were used. Only one Q is described, with no error bars and no seeds.
- Whether T_k is recomputed per rotated direction. This is implied by Sec. 2.2 but not stated for the rotated case.
- The number or fraction of rotated directions that are detectors. Only unique-concept counts are given.

**Human evaluation (Sec. 3.1, Table 3).**
- Setup: Amazon Mechanical Turk raters on AlexNet-Places205 units only. They saw 15 images with the most highly activating patches highlighted and answered yes/no to whether a phrase describes most of the patches.
- There is no random-direction or rotated-basis arm in the human evaluation. The units-vs-rotation comparison uses only the automatic IoU metric.

**GoogLeNet.** It appears only in the architecture comparison: trained from scratch on ImageNet, Places205 and Places365, dissected at the last conv layer, with examples from inception_4e and inception_5b in Fig. 6. GoogLeNet was never rotated.

read:bau2017.bearing:
**Headline.** Bau et al. ask our question (are units more interpretable than random directions?) and answer yes, a privileged basis: their Hypothesis 2. They reject Szegedy et al.'s claim of "no distinction" (their Hypothesis 1). Taken at face value, this disagrees with our pre-ReLU InceptionV1 result, where units and random unit-norm directions score alike: mixed5b 0.57 vs 0.68, mixed4c 0.79 vs 0.74. But the paper's evidence measures something different on almost every axis, so it does not directly contradict our result.

**Where the two studies differ.**
1. **Metric.** Their metric is automatic. It measures spatial IoU between the top 0.5% activation region and pixel masks from a fixed Broden vocabulary. Ours is an open-vocabulary, image-level judgment of 28 top crops plus a held-out discrimination test. A direction with "one job" for a concept Broden lacks scores zero for them; the paper says so itself ("if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, then it will not score well").
2. **Statistic.** Their statistic is layer-level: the count of distinct concepts matched by any of the 256 directions. Ours is a per-direction rate. The paper never reports how many rotated directions are detectors, only unique concepts. An 80% drop in unique concepts could partly mean that mixed directions converge on fewer distinct concepts, not only that each direction is less interpretable. So it does not give a per-direction "one job" rate to compare with our 0.57/0.68 or 0.79/0.74.
3. **No human test of random directions.** Their only human study (Table 3: 15 patches per unit, yes/no on a phrase) covers units only. The paper contains no human or description-based test of random directions. That is exactly the comparison our audit makes, so on that comparison the paper is silent rather than contrary.
4. **Model and scope.** The rotation is run on a single model and layer: AlexNet-Places205 conv5, 256 units, trained from scratch, with one Q draw and no error bars. GoogLeNet was dissected but never rotated, so the paper has no evidence on InceptionV1 mixed4c or mixed5b. The introduction's general wording ("show that emergent interpretability is an axis-aligned property ... destroyed by rotation") rests on that one AlexNet experiment.
5. **Pre- vs post-ReLU.** The paper says only "Denoting AlexNet conv5 as f(x)" and does not say whether that is before or after the ReLU. If it is post-ReLU (common for Caffe conv5 blobs, but not stated here), it lines up with our post-ReLU control, where random directions score lower on the held-out description test. That would be partial agreement. Our pre-ReLU parity has no counterpart in the paper.
6. **Direction distribution.** Each row of their Haar Q is a uniform random unit-norm direction, the same marginal distribution as ours. Their 256 directions are exactly orthogonal; our 40 independent draws in 512 or 1024 dimensions are nearly so. The difference between the studies is therefore the metric, model and layer, not the sampling.
7. **Size of rotation.** From my reading of Fig. 4, rotations of alpha = 0.2 and 0.4 leave unique detectors essentially unchanged (about 79, 81, 77). The collapse comes only at alpha of 0.6 to 1 (about 63, 24, 16). Their claim is about rotations far from the identity, which is the regime of our random directions.

**Overlap check.** Our finding that the random directions' top-16 images are not any single unit's (median overlap 2 of 16) rules out the trivial explanation that a random direction merely inherits one dominant unit. The paper has no corresponding check.

**What to cite it for.** It is the canonical citation for the privileged-basis view. It also offers the batch-norm-whitening intuition for how a privileged basis can be erased. It should be cited as showing an IoU-based, unique-concept-count advantage for units over rotated bases in AlexNet conv5. It does not show that individual random directions look less monosemantic to human or LLM raters.
read:bau2017.caveats:

- **Unreported details:** whether conv5 is taken before or after the ReLU, how many random rotations were drawn, and whether T_k is recomputed per rotated direction. None of these are stated.

read:elhage2022.method:
This is a toy-model paper with no human or LLM interpretability ratings, and it never runs a real-network control against random directions or a rotated basis.

Data: synthetic sparse features. Each x_i is 0 with probability S and otherwise drawn from U[0,1] (U[-1,1] for the absolute-value task). Each feature has an importance I_i, and the loss is importance-weighted MSE.

Models:
(1) Linear model, h=Wx, x'=W^T W x+b.
(2) "ReLU output model", h=Wx, x'=ReLU(W^T W x+b). It has no privileged hidden basis: any orthogonal O with W'=OW gives an identical model.
(3) "ReLU hidden layer" model, h=ReLU(Wx), x'=ReLU(W^T h+b). This is their privileged-basis model. Here W can be read directly as a map from features to neurons.
(4) Absolute-value computation model, h=ReLU(W1 x), y'=ReLU(W2 h+b), with untied weights. The target is y=|x|.

How they measure:
- Whether a feature is represented: ||W_i||.
- Interference: sum_{j≠i}(Ŵ_i·W_j)^2.
- Number of features learned: ||W||_F^2. Dimensions per feature: D*=m/||W||_F^2.
- Per-feature dimensionality: D_i=||W_i||^2 / sum_j(Ŵ_i·W_j)^2.
- Phase diagrams: compare empirical training against closed-form losses of candidate weight configurations.

How a neuron is classed as monosemantic or polysemantic: from the known ground-truth weights, i.e. whether a neuron stores more than one feature, shown in stacked weight plots. In the absolute-value model the faint neuron shading is "judged by eye based on the plots".

"Random" and "rotation" in the paper appear only in two places:
(a) A thought experiment: apply a random invertible linear map M to a word embedding and M^{-1} to the next weights. The model is unchanged, so basis directions are not special. This defines a non-privileged basis.
(b) Toy model (2) is exactly rotation-invariant, since (OW)^T(OW)=W^T W.

No random directions are drawn, and no rotated bases of a trained network are tested for interpretability. InceptionV1 is discussed only qualitatively, with no numbers.
numbers: Intro toy model: 5 features embedded in 2 dimensions with a ReLU afterwards.

Basic results: n=20 features, m=5 hidden dims, I_i=0.7^i. The linear model learns the top-m features. The ReLU output model matches it when dense (1-S=1.0) and goes into superposition as sparsity rises.
Larger basic model: m=20 hidden dims, n=80 features, I_i=0.9^i. The result is 'essentially a rescaled version' of the n=20, m=5 result.

Phase change: 2 features in 1 hidden dim. Feature 1 has importance 1.0; the extra feature's importance ranges from 0.1 to 10; sparsity ranges from 1.0 to 0.01. They train ten models per point, average them, and discard the highest-loss model. Repeated for 3 features in 2 dims.
Uniform superposition: n=400 features, m=30 hidden dims, I_i=1. D*=m/||W||_F^2 is 'sticky' at 1 and 1/2.

Feature dimensionality lines: 3/4 (tetrahedron), 2/3 (triangle), 1/2 (antipodal pair), 2/5 (pentagon), 3/8 (square antiprism), 0 (not learned). The paper says a line at 1 (dedicated dimension) would also appear 'if not for the fact that basis features are indistinguishable from other directions in the dense regime'.
Perturbing one feature: n=5, m=2, I=1, 1-S=0.05 gives a regular pentagon. Off-circle points have ||W_i|| = 1/(1-b_i).
Correlated features: six features in three correlated pairs (m=2). Learning dynamics: n=6, m=3, as two sets of 3 correlated features.

Adversarial: L2 attacks with max norm 0.1 of the average input norm. ReLU neurons are in the zero regime 99% of the time for extremely sparse inputs. Vulnerability rises by more than 3x as superposition forms. Adversarial training fully removed superposition only with attacks at 80% of input L2 norm.
Privileged-basis (ReLU hidden layer) toy: n=10, m=5, I_i=0.75^i. For each model shown, 1000 models were trained and the lowest-loss one visualized. Neuron order was chosen by hand.
Absolute-value model: n=3 features on m=6 neurons (2 neurons per feature without superposition). Superposition sweep: n=100 features, m=40 neurons, I_i=0.8^i, with nonzero x drawn from U[-1,1].
Almost-orthogonal vectors: exp(n) vectors with less than epsilon cosine similarity fit in n dimensions (Johnson-Lindenstrauss).
Compressed-sensing bound: recovery possible iff m = Omega(k log(n/k)). In the toy setting this becomes m = Omega(-n(1-S) log(1-S)).

Strategic picture: features for modestly known people occur with frequency 'significantly less than one in a million tokens'. Sparse coding of a large LM would start from 'millions (neurons) by billions (tokens)', factored 'a thousand or more times larger'.
Nonlinear compression appendix: 12 neurons per Z segment, so it only beats linear compression at a combined 36 neurons. It outperforms linear compression even with epsilon 0.1 and Z=3.
No number is given for the fraction of polysemantic neurons in InceptionV1. The paper says only that it 'increases with depth'.
No unit-vs-random-direction or unit-vs-rotated-basis interpretability number appears anywhere in the paper.

read:elhage2022.bearing:
Overall: the paper measures something different from us, and it does not contradict our finding. Its framework allows our result, and in places predicts it. A few of its unquantified general statements are in mild tension with it.

(1) Definition, not evidence. The paper defines a privileged basis: an architectural feature, such as a coordinatewise activation function, that makes basis directions special and "potentially" encourages features to align with them. It is explicit that this is a precondition, not a guarantee: "having a privileged basis doesn't guarantee that features will be basis-aligned – we'll see that they often aren't! But it's a minimal condition for the question to even make sense." The paper never tests whether units in a trained real network are more interpretable than random directions or a rotated basis. Its only rotation results are:
- the thought experiment with a random invertible M on word embeddings;
- the exact rotation invariance of its no-hidden-nonlinearity toy model, W'=OW.
Its evidence for neuron alignment comes from toy models with known ground-truth features, where monosemanticity is read from weights, partly "judged by eye". So it cannot be cited as showing InceptionV1 units beat random directions. Our audit is a test the paper did not run.

(2) Our directions in the paper's terms. The pre-ReLU concatenated channels of mixed4c/mixed5b form a privileged basis in the paper's sense, because the channel ReLU acts coordinatewise on exactly those coordinates. Our random unit-norm directions are the "any other possible direction" the paper contrasts with neurons. The framework therefore predicts units beat random directions only to the extent that features are basis-aligned rather than in superposition.

(3) Mid-to-late InceptionV1 layers. The paper's own qualitative claims point toward heavy superposition there:
- "the fraction of neurons which are polysemantic in InceptionV1 increases with depth";
- "superposition and polysemanticity increase as sparsity increases";
- its clean-neuron examples are from "early" InceptionV1 (curve detectors, Zoom In).
Our parity on the 'one job' rating (mixed5b 0.57 units vs 0.68 random; mixed4c 0.79 vs 0.74) is what the paper's theory allows if features in these layers are largely not basis-aligned. It is in mild tension with the unquantified general statements "Often, these neurons correspond to interpretable features" and "many neurons just cleanly respond to features". The paper gives no numbers that could refute our parity.

(4) Top-crop ratings may be weak. The paper's absolute-value toy shows neurons with a large-weight "primary" feature plus smaller "secondary" ones, whose largest activations are "all or nearly-all" the primary feature while lower activations are polysemantic. It links this to LM neurons that "appear interpretable when we examine their strongest activations". This means a rater who sees only the top 28 dataset-example crops samples the regime where even polysemantic units look like they have one job.

My inference, not stated in the paper: under sparse superposition, a random direction's top activations could likewise be dominated by whichever sparse feature projects most onto it. That would make 'one job' ratings from top crops weak at telling units from random directions. Our median top-16 overlap of 2/16 with any single unit shows the random directions are not copies of units. That fits them picking up different features, but the paper does not test this.

(5) Pre-ReLU versus post-ReLU random directions. The paper does not address this split; the following is my inference only. A random direction over pre-ReLU channels is itself a linear template over the previous layer's rectified features. The paper describes neurons as "pattern match[ing] a particular weight template", so such a direction is the same kind of object as a unit's pre-activation, lacking only the coordinatewise ReLU and trained bias. A random direction over post-ReLU outputs instead mixes the rectified outputs of many units. That is plausibly closer to a union of several units' features, which would fit its lower held-out description score. The paper's own discussion of ReLU filtering only covers interference in its toy output layer.

(6) Bottom line. The paper supplies the concept our control tests: privileged basis as a necessary, not sufficient, condition for neurons to be special. It offers no empirical claim, number or method that units are more interpretable than random or rotated directions in a real CNN. Our result is evidence about the question the paper says only "makes sense" to ask in a privileged basis, and the answer it gives (little or no unit advantage at mixed4c and mixed5b on the one-job rating) is permitted by the paper's superposition account.
read:elhage2022.caveats:
- Toy models only. Features are synthetic and independent (apart from deliberately correlated sets), and ground truth is known. The authors write that "it's very unclear what to generalize to real networks".
- The privileged-basis toy (ReLU hidden layer) has a weakness the paper admits: it "will only use the ReLU activation function if absolutely forced". The cleaner privileged-basis evidence comes from the absolute-value model.
- Monosemanticity in the paper is defined from weights, not from dataset examples or raters. The neuron shading in the absolute-value figure is "judged by eye".
- InceptionV1 claims (clean early neurons; polysemantic fraction rising with depth) are stated without numbers or method in this paper; they cite Circuits work (Cammarata et al. 2020, "Curve Detectors"; Olah et al. 2020, "Zoom In").
- The "longer discussion" of privileged bases the paper points to is in a different paper, SoLU (Elhage et al. 2022, section 3.2), at https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/solu/index.html#section-3-2. I did not read it.
- Figures are embedded raster images. I read all text, captions and footnotes but could not extract values plotted inside the figures, such as the phase diagrams or stacked weight plots.
- The arXiv PDF is v1 (21 Sep 2022) and differs slightly from the current HTML. In particular the disentanglement sentence about privileged bases is worded differently; both versions are quoted. All other quotes are from the current HTML.
- "[cite]" marks where I removed an inline citation from a quote. Nothing else in the quotes is altered.
- Points (4) partly, and (5) entirely, in the bearing are my inferences and are labelled as such. They are not claims the paper makes.

read:fong2018.method:
What they measured: how well single filters versus learned linear combinations of all filters in a layer detect labelled concepts. They did not measure interpretability as rated by people, and they did not test whether units are more interpretable than random directions.

Probe data: BRODEN, with more than 60,000 images and 1197 concepts. They dropped 8 scene concepts that had no validation examples, leaving 1189 concepts for classification. Of these, 682 have pixel masks and are used for segmentation (no scenes or textures).

Main network and layers: AlexNet trained on ImageNet, layers conv1 to conv5 (64/192/384/256/256 filters). Other networks: VGG16 conv5_3; GoogLeNet inception5b, plus inception4c, 4e and 5a in the supplement; each trained on ImageNet and on Places365. Also conv5 of five self-supervised AlexNets (tracking, audio, objectcentric, moving, egomotion). The paper does not say which GoogLeNet checkpoint it used. Activations are taken after the ReLU.

(1) Single filter (a modified NetDissect): each filter k is thresholded at its top-0.005 activation quantile T_k, computed over all probe images and positions. The mask is thresholded before bilinear upsampling. Set IoU is computed against the concept mask. The best filter is picked on the train split and scored on val.

(2) Segmentation by combination: M(x;w) = sigmoid(sum_k w_k * I(A_k(x) > T_k)). This is a weighted sum of per-unit thresholded indicators, so the unit basis is built into the input. It is trained with a size-weighted per-pixel BCE loss (SGD, lr 1e-4, momentum 0.9, batch 64, 30 epochs) and the output is thresholded at 1/2.

(3) Classification: f(x) = sigmoid(b + sum_k w_k * spatial-mean A_k(x)). Training uses positive/negative sets sampled in balance (lr 1e-1, dropped to 1e-2 after epoch 15, momentum 0.9, batch 64, 30 epochs). It is scored by accuracy on a balanced validation set.

(4) Top-F subsets (following Agrawal et al.): keep the F filters with the largest |w_k| and retrain on them. Classification uses F in {1,2,3,5,10,...,128}; conv5 segmentation uses F in {1,2,4,...,224}.

(5) Sharing: count how many concepts pick each filter as their best filter.

(6) Non-maximal visualisation: show one example at each decile of the nonzero part of the per-image IoU distribution.

(7) Correlation between max(w,0) and each unit's set IoU.

(8) The learned w, scaled to unit length, used as concept embeddings: nearest neighbours by cosine similarity, vector arithmetic, K-means and t-SNE, and distances between networks and to WordNet/Word2Vec.

The paper draws no random directions, random rotations or random bases anywhere. The only mention of a random basis is a one-sentence citation of Szegedy et al. 2014 in Related Work.

read:fong2018.bearing:
Overall, the paper measures something different from our audit and never tests the claim we tested. It gives indirect support to our finding on several points and offers only weak, untested hints the other way.

(1) No random-direction or rotation control. Net2Vec never draws random directions or random rotations, and it never asks whether units are more interpretable than other directions. Its only comparison is a single unit (one-hot w) against a supervised linear combination learned for each concept on BRODEN labels. A learned direction is a much stronger rival than our random unit-norm directions, so "learned combinations beat the best unit on 76-92% of concepts (segmentation) and 85-90% (classification)" says the unit axes are not the best readouts for labelled concepts. It says nothing on whether units beat random directions. Nothing in the paper says units are more interpretable than random or rotated directions.

(2) Prior evidence the paper cites. The paper's only sentence on a random basis cites Szegedy et al. 2014: top patches along random-basis directions are also semantically coherent. That is the earlier version of our result. Net2Vec quotes it as a contrast to single-filter claims and does not dispute or re-test it.

(3) Points consistent with our finding. Filters are rarely exclusive: about 15% of conv1 filters are the best filter for at least 20 or 30 concepts, and 13 conv5 filters exceed IoU 0.15 on several concepts. Filters are not sufficient on their own. The authors frame the representation as "at least in part distributed". This fits our result that units were not rated 'one job' more often than random directions (mixed5b 0.57 vs 0.68; mixed4c 0.79 vs 0.74). Two differences: their polysemanticity is measured against BRODEN labels with a quantile threshold, not by raters; and many of their multi-concept units cover related concepts ('animal torso': sheep, cow, horse) that a rater might still call one job.

(4) Points that could cut the other way, all untested against a random baseline:
(a) Concept readouts are fairly sparse in the unit basis. Segmentation peaks at F = 8-16 filters for parts, materials and objects, and classification saturates by about F = 50 of 256.
(b) Learned weights track each unit's own IoU (rho = 0.92 for dog, 0.87 for airplane; 47-82% of concepts significant).
(c) In GoogLeNet-ImageNet, the best single filter nearly matches the learned combination for objects at inception5b (about 0.141 vs 0.144 set IoU) and beats it for parts at 4c, 4e, 5a and 5b.

These suggest units carry concept signal that is concentrated along the axes, which is a weak hint of a privileged basis. But three things weaken each hint. First, there is no random-rotation null. Second, all inputs are post-ReLU. Third, the segmentation combination is a weighted sum of per-unit thresholded indicators I(A_k > T_k), so the unit basis is built into the method. The GoogLeNet result is also confounded by the combination overfitting at 7x7 resolution, which the paper itself discusses.

Their post-ReLU, per-unit thresholded setting matches our post-ReLU condition, where random directions also scored lower on the held-out test. It does not match our pre-ReLU condition, where units and random directions were rated alike. So there is no direct conflict with our results.

(5) Implication for our method. Section 5.1 shows that single units look clean in their top-activating examples but often fall apart at lower deciles (many IoU_ind = 0; 'train' first appears at rank 27 for its best filter). Our audit rates top crops (28 crops, plus 8 held-out top crops among 16), which is the regime the paper warns "can favor easy-to-interpret cases". This bias could inflate units and random directions alike, so it does not overturn our equality result. It does suggest re-running the unit-vs-random comparison on crops sampled by decile.

(6) The 2-of-16 overlap figure. The paper has no overlap statistic between the top images of a direction and those of a unit. It only shows qualitatively that the images best aligned with the learned weights differ from the best filter's (supplement Figs 13-14).
read:fong2018.caveats:
- Many numbers above (Figs 2, 3 and 5; supplement Figs 10 and 11) are my own approximate readings of bar and line charts. The paper does not state them.
- The GoogLeNet in the paper is described only as "GoogLeNet [19] inception5b trained on ImageNet [16] and Places365 [25]". It is most likely the Caffe/NetDissect models, not TF inception5h. Their inception5b and inception4c correspond to our mixed5b and mixed4c in layer name only; the trained units are not the same.
- Inconsistencies in the source:
  - The Fig 7 caption says 'train' for the right panel, but the plot shows 'airplane' (N = 184, filter 144).
  - Supplement text says "filter 428", but Fig 9 labels it filter 248, and conv5 has only 256 filters.
  - Table 1 percentages differ slightly from supplement Figs 5 and 6 (for example, segmentation conv5 75.7 vs 75.95, classification conv5 88.1 vs 88.81), and the supplement Fig 5 caption says 'training set'.
  - The supplement cites "main fig. 4" for the filter-sharing counts, which are in main Fig 5.
  - The heading of Appendix B.1 calls the 682 segmentation concepts "classification concepts".
- The paper has no human or LLM ratings, no 'one job' style judgement and no held-out description test. Its interpretability evidence is IoU and accuracy against BRODEN labels plus qualitative figures.
- Single-filter and combination counts in supplement Fig 10 use different IoU thresholds (0.04 vs 0.20), so they cannot be compared directly.
- Selecting the "best single filter" means taking the maximum over K units on train. Any comparison to random directions would need the same best-of-K selection; the paper does not do this.

The reader quotes both sentences elsewhere. The Introduction also says "random projections of φ(x)". wrong: No outright misquotes or wrong numbers. I fetched arXiv 1704.05796v1 myself (9 pages; v1 is the only version; the comment matches) and checked all 25 quotes against the extracted text with a script. All are verbatim, including the paper's own slips "count the number unique concepts" and "a combination of a several hidden units". The math was re-typed ("Qf(x)" for "Qf (x)", "Q^α" for "Qα"), which the reader disclosed. Every Table 1, Table 3, Fig. 3, Fig. 6, Sec. 3.5, Sec. 3.7 and Fig. 10 number listed is correct. The items below are imprecise or overstated rather than false.

Method, IoU: "IoU_{k,c} = sum|M_k ∩ L_c| / sum|M_k ∪ L_c| over the whole dataset" is imprecise. Sec. 2.2 says "the sums are computed only on the subset of images that have at least one labeled concept of the same category as c."

Bearing point 4 says "with one Q draw and no error bars" as if it were fact. The paper only describes "a random orthogonal transformation Q" and never gives the number of draws, which the reader's own method section states correctly ("Only one Q is described"). The later TPAMI version (arXiv 1711.05611v2) says the full rotation was repeated 10 times.

Bearing point 1 says a direction coding for a concept Broden lacks "scores zero for them". The paper says only that it "will not score well for interpretability". Such a direction can still pass IoU > 0.04 on some other Broden label and be counted.

Caveat on GoogLeNet: "trained from scratch by the authors" and "They are not Google's inception5h weights" are inferences. The paper says only that the supervised models "are trained from scratch (i.e., not pretrained)". It does not say who trained them or which weight release was used.

Random-weights baseline, missed entirely. Table 2 lists AlexNet-random (training: none), and Figs. 7 and 8 show it has only 2 unique detectors at conv5, both texture. The fully rotated Places205 conv5 (16) is therefore far above an untrained network. It sits at about the level of the weaker self-supervised AlexNets in Fig. 8: puzzle 16, egomotion 15, moving 18, colorization 18, context 8, frameorder 4; tracking scores 41. Rotation reduces the count; it does not make it random-like.

Fig. 11 gives the training-condition counts the reader said were absent (exact from the vector data). Unique detectors: baseline 79, Repeat1 85, Repeat2 85, Repeat3 83, NoDropout 68, BatchNorm 46, so BatchNorm has about 42% fewer than baseline, compared with 80% for full rotation. So the method is not limited to the unique-concept statistic; the paper simply did not report it for the rotation. Fig. 11 shows unique and total counts moving together across training conditions.

Sec. 3.6 and Fig. 12, discrimination vs interpretability: across representations there is a 'positive correlation' between the number of unique object detectors and linear-SVM accuracy on action40, and supervised and self-supervised models 'form two clusters'.
